first.text: The ferry-master is a square old woman in a sea-dark greatcoat, a brass hand-scale hanging from one fist. She looks at the ember in your hand for a long moment, then up at the Gull.
Oda Farrow. Master of the Slow Mercy, thirty-eight years on the lanes. We saw your light from the Narrows. Whole crew stood at the rail like fools.
You'll know we don't take coin. The lanes want a deed, and I weigh it. That's the fare, the old way.
So. Tell it me. What did you do here?

choice.text: Saltmarrow relit it. I carried the ember up the hill.
Does it matter? I need to cross.

deed_claimed.text: Plain enough. I like a plain teller.

deed_shared.text: Hah. A Wakebearer who shares the weight. That's new. The lanes like that — they're shared, too.

deed_brusque.text: It matters to the lanes. Might be it'll matter to you, the far side of the fog.

cost.text: A beacon doesn't light for nothing. What did it eat?

cost_pebble.text: A lullaby. Saltmarrow's cradle-song. Nobody here can hum it now.
That one? I've heard it sung off this very dock. Went like—
She hums. Three notes, four. They go past you like rain off a coat; you reach for them and there is nothing to hold.
…You didn't catch that, did you. None of you will. Burned is burned, for them that stood in the light.
I'll keep it, then. Somebody should.

cost_knot.text: Saltmarrow's founding knot. The first knot of the first net.
Oda's jaw works. Behind her, a deckhand coiling rope stops coiling.
Every Tidewright net starts with a knot someone taught us. I'll not pretend that sits easy with my crew.
But the Gull's lit, and the lanes can see Saltmarrow again. That weighs more. Barely.

cost_gull.text: A memory of Mara's. Of someone she loved. I— can't recall who.
Mara Tollen's? Then it'll be Dunstan. Her brother. Big laugh, bigger hands. Crewed for me two winters, and sang worse than the horn.
The name goes past you like a gull past a window. You try to hold it, and there is nothing there to hold.
…You don't know him. None of you do, now. I'll not say it again; it's a cruelty, saying it.

weigh.text: Oda sets something you can't see on one pan of her scale, and waits. The pans rock, and settle level.
Hm. You tell it poorly. The deed's heavier than the telling, so it'll do.
It weighs. You've a berth on the Slow Mercy.
Not to Cindermoor. Nobody lands on Cindermoor, not since the Spire went dark. The lanes run light to light, and the next light's out. Thornwold. I'll take you that far.

choice.text: Why only as far as Thornwold?
The big man from the rowboat had word for you.
Dunstan's staying on the fen. Turning the long walk's boards round.
The big man from the rowboat is staying on the fen, turning the boards round.
I've brought the big man's answer.

route.text: Tidewright lanes run beacon to beacon. A lit island is a lane you can steer by. A dark one's a hole in the sea.
Thornwold's beacon went out the night of the Snuffing, same as yours. Pines and bramble, and paths that won't lie still. The charcoal folk are still there, and our lumber camp, what's left of it.
Light Thornwold, and the lane past it opens, and the one past that. That's the way toward Cindermoor: one light at a time, same as anyone.

sleeve.text: Oda looks at the faded thread for a long time. She does not touch it.
Keepers ride my deck if they pay. They pay twice: once for the crossing, and once for the Spire. It went dark on their watch.
Aldous Wren cut that off himself? Then he's done one honest thing in his life. Keep it in your coat. My crew won't be so thoughtful.

pell.text: The kid on my dock with the bundle says they're crossing with you. Children cross with their kin's leave. That's lane law, old as the lanes.
Get Mara Tollen's say, or leave the kid on the dock. I'll not steal a child off an island, even for a Wakebearer.
Mara's said yes? Then the kid crosses. I'll put them to coiling rope. Kids who coil rope don't fall overboard.
The kid's sat on that bundle an hour, not crying. Hard thing, a promise taken back. The lanes weigh those too, you know.

ready.text: Not while that kid's waiting on an answer. Go and get Mara's say, one way or the other.
Oda puts two fingers in her mouth and whistles. Aboard the Slow Mercy, somebody starts counting the tide.
Evening tide, then. Say what's left to say. When you step aboard, you're ours till Thornwold.

sail.text: Oda puts two fingers in her mouth and whistles. The plank comes in, the lines come off the posts, and the Slow Mercy leans away from the dock on the evening tide.
Mara stands at the end of the dock with the green lantern held up, and does not wave until you do.
Mara stands at the end of the dock with the green lantern held up. Behind her, by the worn stool, two cups are set out. She waves to you, and only to you.
Pell is at the rail beside you with a coil of rope going wrong in both hands, waving at Mara until the lantern is a green spark.
At the dock's end Pell cups both hands and shouts something across the water. It might be "something GOOD".
Pell sits on the packed bundle at the foot of the dock and doesn't wave. Then, when you have almost gone, does.
Pell runs the length of the dock beside you, waving with both arms, and stops at the very last plank.
The Gull's Beacon burns on its headland behind you. Oda keeps it dead astern and counts under her breath. The lanes run light to light, and ahead there is no light at all.
Down on the deck a crewman hums while he coils a line: a lullaby, slow, with a turn at the end. You try to keep hold of it and it goes past you like rain off a coat.
A deckhand makes fast a line with a knot you almost know, the way you almost know a word. Then it is only a knot.
Oda says a name to the wind, quietly: an old crewmate's. It does not stay with you.
The fog closes over the Gull's light. The ember in your hand is the only colour left on the sea.
Steady. A dark island's a hole in the sea, but holes have edges. Listen for the trees.
And then you can: pines, a long way off, breathing.

sail_again.text: Oda casts off without ceremony. One end of the lane is lit now; she steers off the Gull and counts the rest of the way to the pines.

thornwold.text: Two lit. The Gull astern of us one way, the Ridge Light the other. That's a lane you can count on.

And it's the start of another. North-about from here lies Glasswater Fen. Dark, last I heard, and strange with it. Steer with the Ridge Light dead astern and listen for reeds instead of trees. When you've a mind to, and I've a tide.
Off-islanders, my crew. We'll still have what Thornwold burned. Don't ask us to tell you. It slides off.
You carried the Lamp's name home off the Book. Wenna let you read it, so that's between you and the Book.
But you're ours now, sworn. The Book doesn't mind being read. It minds being emptied. Don't make a habit of carrying fares back, friend of the lanes.
You carried the Lamp's name home off the Book. A Keeper's fare, given back by somebody who's not one of ours. Wenna'll not mind. She'd mind if you were sworn.
You read a fare and left it paid. Tidewright manners, that. Wenna would weigh you heavy for it.

choice.text: The big man from the rowboat had word for you.
Dunstan's staying on the fen. Turning the long walk's boards round.
The big man from the rowboat is staying on the fen, turning the boards round.
I've brought the big man's answer.

thornwold_keeper.text: A Keeper. Thirty years up at the light, by the camp's count. Never rode my deck, not once. Never left the island, that one.
Ask Bram. He keeps tallies of everything, even the things he says he doesn't believe.

sleeve_thornwold.text: Oda looks at the faded thread for a long time. She does not touch it.
Put that away. Keepers ride my deck if they pay, and they pay twice. On Thornwold, I'd not show it to the camp.

back.text: The lane to the Gull's an easy one. Lit at one end; that's all a lane needs.
The Slow Mercy crosses back on the Gull's light, and Saltmarrow's stilts come up out of the grey one by one.

sail_fen.text: Oda casts off on the ebb and takes the Slow Mercy north-about, round Thornwold's shoulder, with the Ridge Light dead astern.
Pell watches from the jetty with a fistful of Bram's nails and doesn't ask to come. Thornwold has given them work, and work is a kind of staying.
The gold of the Ridge Light shrinks to a spark, and the spark to a warmth you remember more than see. Oda counts. Then she stops counting, and listens.
Hear that? Like somebody breathing out through their teeth. That's reeds. Reeds, and no wind in them.
The fog here is different. It doesn't drift. It hangs, as if the sea had stopped to listen too.
Glasswater. Fen folk used to meet every boat with a lantern on a pole. Nobody's met a boat here since the Snuffing, that I've heard.

sail_fen_again.text: Oda takes the Slow Mercy north-about again with the Ridge Light astern, until the reeds start breathing.

fen.text: Three lit. The Gull, the Ridge Light, and that heron on stilts. I'd not have wagered on the heron.
We'll lie here a tide or two. I don't like water that doesn't move. Water that doesn't move is thinking.

choice.text: That rowboat tied at the staithe...
I went out to the Heron's legs.
I found the big man from the rowboat.
Where does the lane go from here?
The big man from the rowboat had word for you.
Dunstan's staying on the fen. Turning the long walk's boards round.
The big man from the rowboat is staying on the fen, turning the boards round.
I've brought the big man's answer.

fen_rowboat.text: Saltmarrow-built. Tollen-built, by the stem: old Tollen cut his stems a hand proud, so you'd know them in the dark. Dunstan's, then.
He crewed for me two winters. Best hand on a line I ever had, and he laughed at weather. I'd not have thought it of him, rowing off into this.
The name goes past you like rain off a coat.
You've a look like I said nothing. That'll be the Gull's burn. Never mind it.

fen_back.text: Ridge Light dead ahead, this way. Easier, steering toward a light.
The reeds close behind the Slow Mercy, and in a while the fog ahead goes faintly gold.

fen_heron.text: Out to the legs, in an eel-punt, in that? Rather you than me.
You tied her bell back on her bow. Good. A boat ought to say she's coming in, whether or not anyone's listening.
You kept her bell. Don't ring it on my deck. A ship's bell rung where there's no ship calls the wrong things in.
And you called him, and he went on. He did that on deck when he'd made his mind up: say his name and he'd keep coiling.
And you let him walk. Some would have shouted. I might have.
And you saw a big man you couldn't put a name to. I could. I won't. It'd only run off you.

fen_dunstan.text: Then he's all right. Or he will be. That man laughed at weather.
A gull for Mara? I'll carry it the long way round, Thornwold and the Gull. It'll keep. Gulls do.
He's sat by a lantern with nobody to tell him the tide. Well. He knows the tide.

fen_lane.text: East-about. Keep the Heron astern and the morning on your right cheek, the old pilots say, and you raise Wrackholm in a day.
Our yards. Tidewright salvage, and the lane-house where the masters are sworn. Where they swore me, thirty-eight years back.
Dark. Nobody's answered a horn from Wrackholm since the Snuffing, and that's not like us. We answer horns.
Cindermoor's past it, and past more besides. That's how it goes.
Not this tide. When I sail for Wrackholm I want my crew rested and you done here. You've a look like you're not.
You've the look of somebody done here, near enough. Say the word, and we'll go east-about.

sail_wrackholm.text: Oda takes the Slow Mercy out of the reeds on the morning ebb and puts her east-about, the Heron's gold astern and the low sun on your right cheek, the way the old pilots say.
A gull for the stool, facing the door. Not a promise. That's a Tollen for you: he'll tell you what a thing isn't.
You told him about the two cups. Somebody had to. I'm glad it wasn't me.
You told him she's well. That's a message too. The kind a man can carry.
You told him she's well, and not the rest. That's a kindness I'd not have managed.
You carried him nothing of Mara's. Some things don't go in a satchel.
And you asked him what he'd put down, and he didn't know. Good. That's the only answer worth having, out there.
And you never asked him what he'd put down. Tidewright manners. We don't ask a man what's in his hold.
By noon the Heron is a warmth astern and there is nothing ahead but grey. Oda puts the bone horn to her mouth: one long note, then two short. Putting in; passengers welcome.
Nothing answers. She waits as long as it takes to say a name, and blows again. Nothing.
Thirty-eight years I've blown for Wrackholm and been answered before the second short was done. Wenna Garrow swore me master in that lane-house. She'd answer a horn in her sleep.

Oda puts a man in the bows with the lead and comes in slow, by soundings, the way you come into a harbor you can't see. Somewhere off the bow to port the sea breaks on something and draws back, over and over, like breath through teeth.
The Teeth. We keep them to port, and we keep quiet. ...There. Wrackholm.

sail_wrackholm_again.text: Oda takes the Slow Mercy east-about again with the Heron astern, and comes in slow by soundings, the Teeth breathing to port.

wrackholm.text: I'll lie here while I've a tide. I don't like the sound of the Teeth from a harbor nobody answers.
Wenna, still warden. Good. And the Gannet... I knew Hale Corbet. I'll not say more till his name's been said proper.
She said them into the horn? Hale, and Annis, and Ruan Pask. Then they're home. That's the old way.
Four lit. The Gull, the Ridge, that heron, and the Wrack. My grandmother'd have called me a liar.
Wrackholm blew and I answered it. Backwards, but I'll take it. I'd forgotten that horn's voice.
She doesn't remember answering. Fifty years of it. Well, I do; an off-islander keeps what you burn. I'll keep that for her.
Hale, and Annis, and Ruan Pask. Nobody on this hard can say them now. I can. I'll say them at every jetty I tie up at, then.
The Pask lad doesn't remember going out on the Teeth. Hale told it on my deck once: the boy never looked up the whole way.
She swore you. Did you cry? ...I'll not tell.

choice.text: The big man from the rowboat had word for you.
Dunstan's staying on the fen. Turning the long walk's boards round.
The big man from the rowboat is staying on the fen, turning the boards round.
I've brought the big man's answer.
Where does the lane go from here?

wrackholm_wenna.text: Lane-warden. Keeps the lane-house and the horn, and swears the masters. She swore me. I cried. If she tells you that, she's lying.
Eighty if she's a day. She's answered every horn on this hard for fifty years. So something's wrong.

wrackholm_back.text: Heron dead ahead, this way. Easier, steering toward a light.
The Teeth breathe once more astern, and are gone. In a while the grey ahead goes faintly gold, low on the water.

passage_saltmarrow.text: Oda takes the Slow Mercy home the long way, light to light: up the Taper to the Wrack, west-about to the Heron, round Thornwold's shoulder to the Ridge Light, and down the Gull lane. She puts in at the hard, the staithe and the jetty only long enough to take on water.

Oda takes the Slow Mercy home the long way, light to light: west-about to the Heron, round Thornwold's shoulder to the Ridge Light, and down the Gull lane. She puts in at the staithe and the jetty only long enough to take on water.
Oda takes the Slow Mercy home light to light: round Thornwold's shoulder to the Ridge Light, and down the Gull lane. She puts in at the jetty only long enough to take on water.
Every lane's a short one, if it's lit at both ends. It's the dark ones that are long.
Saltmarrow's stilts come up out of the grey one by one, and the Gull burns over them.

passage_thornwold.text: Oda takes the Slow Mercy up the Taper to the Wrack and west-about to the Heron, putting in at the hard and the staithe only long enough to take on water, then back round Thornwold's shoulder with the Heron astern.
Oda takes the Slow Mercy west-about to the Heron and puts in at the staithe only long enough to take on water, then back round Thornwold's shoulder with the Heron astern.
Pines. Hear them? I'd know that breathing in my sleep now.

passage_fen.text: Oda steers off the Gull and up the lane to the Ridge Light, and puts in at Thornwold's jetty only long enough to take on water. Then north-about, until the reeds start breathing.
Oda takes the Slow Mercy up the Taper to the Wrack and puts in at the hard only long enough to take on water. Then west-about, until the reeds start breathing.
Two lanes on one tide. Before the Snuffing that was nothing. Now it's a thing to say out loud.

passage_wrackholm.text: Oda steers off the Gull and sails light to light: the Ridge Light, north-about to the Heron, and east-about with the morning on your right cheek. She puts in at the jetty and the staithe only long enough to take on water.
Oda sails light to light: north-about to the Heron, then east-about with the morning on your right cheek. She puts in at the staithe only long enough to take on water.
She comes in slow by soundings at the last, the Teeth breathing to port, the way she always will.

dunstan_word.text: He's not laughing at the weather. He's laughing at something else.
Oda doesn't answer at once. She looks out past the bow, the way she looks at a sky she's making her mind up about.
Two winters he crewed for me. Every blow we took, he laughed at it like it had told him a joke. I never asked him what at. You don't, on a deck.
Something else. Well. I'll hear what, one day. Not from you. From him, and he'll take a whole tide over the telling.
And his own sister doesn't know his face, and I do. That's the wrong way round. That's the burn's way round.
Tell him his berth's still swung on the Mercy. He'll not take it. Tell him anyway.

dunstan_stayed_word.text: So the near edge sits proud for whoever walks back. He says he's finished forgetting, and somebody may as well start the other thing.
Mending. Out there. The fen won't thank him for it. Nobody thanks you for a board; they only notice the one that tips.
She knocks her knuckles twice on the rail, the way Tidewrights do to close a bargain.

That rowboat of his has sat in still water too long. When he's done, the Mercy calls at the fen. Tell him he rides home on my deck, and no fare. Thirty-eight years sworn and I've never said that to a man. He can have it carved.

dunstan_answer.text: He says no, and thank you, and it's a stool now. He said you'd know what he means by a stool.
Something happens at the corner of her mouth that on anybody else would be a smile.
Aye, I know. A man ought to have one thing that stays where he left it. I'll unswing the berth. Not today.
And if he said anything soft about me knowing his face, you'll have the sense not to bring it aboard. Good.
He'll go home by oar; he came out by oar. But he'll wave from the staithe every time the Mercy goes by, till you're sick of it.
He will, too. I'll have to put the crew to waving back or he'll sulk the length of the fen.
By oar. Tollens. I'll keep the berth swung anyway. It's no weight to me.
That's all the answer it gets. It seems to be enough for both of them.

wrackholm_lane.text: South-about, down the Taper. Keepers' water. They named it for the long thin candles they burn: a day and a night of it, and the old pilots say it's like steering down a wick.

Kindleby at the end of it. The Keepers' mother-house. They'll tell you the Kindling was lit there and rowed out to Cindermoor in an open boat, nine hundred years back. They'll tell you a lot of things.
Keepers pay twice on our decks. On their own island they don't pay at all. I've put in there four times in thirty-eight years, and been thanked every time, and never once been asked in.
You're sworn a friend of the lanes. They'll see the Tidewright on you before they see the ember. Hold your head up.
Say the word and we'll go south-about. The Wrack's lit; nobody'll say I left a dark light astern.

sail_kindleby.text: Oda takes the Slow Mercy off the hard on the ebb and out past the Teeth, the Wrack burning on its stack astern, and puts her south-about down a long grey reach where the water lies very still.
You told the Pask lad Keepers put the Spire out. It's on every deck from here to the Gull by now; Tidewrights talk. I'd not be the one to say it first on Kindleby.
If they ask after Wynn Sallow, you'll tell them, I suppose. Keepers wrote half their beacon-keepers off by spring. Keepers don't like being wrong in ink.
And you've colliers on the Northing's stage to speak for, waiting on the Spire's boat. Somebody's got to tell the Keepers. Might as well be the one with the ember.
Toward evening there's a light ahead. Not one light: dozens, low and yellow, then hundreds, ringing an island like a string of beads. Candles. On a sea wall, on steps, in every window.
Tallow. They're holding the fog off with tallow. ...And look at that, it's working, a bit. A cable's width. That's nine hundred years of practice, that is.
Before Oda can lift the bone horn, a bell rings from the quay: one stroke, then three.
Answered before I've blown. That's Keepers. They've been watching for us. Watching for you, more like.

sail_kindleby_again.text: Oda takes the Slow Mercy south-about down the Taper again, the Wrack astern, until the candles come up out of the grey and the quay bell rings one, then three.

kindleby.text: I'll lie here. Mind they don't keep you. Keepers are hospitable the way a net is hospitable.
Lorn. She was Provost when I was a deckhand. She looked at me then the way she'll have looked at you: like a thing to be put in its right place.
You bowed to their rite. Well. You've chosen four times; maybe you've earned letting somebody else. I'd not. But I'm a Tidewright, and we don't let anybody choose our cargo.
You told Lorn no. I'd have paid to see her face. ...No I wouldn't. I've seen it.
Five lights, and one of them tallow. Don't tell her I counted it.

They've forgotten the boats. I saw them come in, the week of the Snuffing: I was lying off the Taper for the weather, and they rowed past me all night with lanterns in their bows. ...I'll not tell them. It won't stick.
The lad at their bell doesn't remember he was ever going anywhere. Well. Most of us never were.
Five lights. Every one of them yours, whoever did the choosing.
Six lights, and a line on my chart I never thought I'd ink. Every one of them yours.
Morning ebb. I've not changed my mind, if that's what you're asking. I've just not slept.

choice.text: The big man from the rowboat had word for you.
Dunstan's staying on the fen. Turning the long walk's boards round.
The big man from the rowboat is staying on the fen, turning the boards round.
I've brought the big man's answer.
Where does the ring go from here?
Cast off down the lane in.
Take me back in to Cindermoor.

kindleby_back.text: Wrack dead ahead, up the Taper. I'll not pretend I'm sorry to see the candles go astern.
The candles sink into the grey behind, bead by bead, until there's only the one bell, ringing you away: three, then one.

passage_kindleby.text: Oda sails light to light: off the Gull to the Ridge Light, north-about to the Heron, east-about to the Wrack, and south-about down the Taper. She puts in at the jetty, the staithe and the hard only long enough to take on water.
Oda sails light to light: north-about to the Heron, east-about to the Wrack, and south-about down the Taper. She puts in at the staithe and the hard only long enough to take on water.
Oda sails east-about to the Wrack and puts in at the hard only long enough to take on water, then south-about down the Taper.
The candles come up out of the grey at the last, and the quay bell rings one, then three, the way it always will.

kindleby_low_water.text: From here? Back up the Taper, the way we came. That's the ring, near enough: five lights and the Gull, and Cindermoor dark in the middle.
She looks south, past the candles, where the grey goes on.

Near enough. There's water between here and the Gull that nobody sails. The Low Water. On the old charts it's a scatter of rock, and between the rocks the sea's so shallow you'd think you could wade it. Pilots went round. Even before the Snuffing, they went round.

choice.text: Is there a light out there?

low_water_sings.text: Because it sings. The fog. Out there you can hear it: voices, near enough, a lot of them, none of them saying anything you can catch. Ferrymen won't sail what they can hear and can't see. Not my grandmother, and not me.

The old pilots call it the Choir. The Hollow Choir. You'll hear that on any deck after the second bottle: it's the drowned, or the Hushed gone out over the water, or it's the wind in the skerries. I've heard it. It's not the wind.

low_water_light.text: Was. The old charts have one: a Keepers' light on the biggest of the rocks. Keepers' water, that; they rowed it out to their own, and we went round. I couldn't tell you who keeps it. I couldn't tell you if anybody does, now.
And before you ask why we went round: it sings. The fog out there. Voices, near enough, a lot of them. Ferrymen won't sail what they can hear and can't see.

low_water_chart.text: You held their whole ring with that ember for an hour. I've a deckhand says you'd hold the Low Water off too. I've a deckhand who talks too much.
Oda takes the chart out of her coat, wets a thumb on the ink-stick and smudges a patch of grey into the gap south of the ring, and a few dots in it for the rocks.
There. It's on the chart. I'll not sail it. The Mercy draws too much for that water anyway, and she's got more sense than I have.
If you want rowing out there, ask a Keeper. They've a skiff on that shingle, when it's home, and they've never been afraid of anything but being wrong.

lights_between.text: Oda is at the rail with her glass to her eye, looking south past the candles. She doesn't put it down when you come aboard.
There's a light on the Low Water. Gold. It came up off the end of the candles while you were out there, small as a pin, and it hasn't gone out.
And there's a Keeper on the chapter-house steps who wasn't on them yesterday, and Lorn's been at him in front of everybody. I'll not ask.
Somebody's keeping it, too. You don't get a light that steady by leaving it.
She lowers the glass and counts on her fingers, the way she counted fares on the Gull's dock.
The Gull. The Ridge Light. The Heron. The Wrack. Their tallow up on the crown. And that. Six.
She takes the chart out of her coat and spreads it on the deckhouse roof, a fist on each corner. The lights go round Cindermoor in a ring, and for the first time there's no gap in it.

The lights between. That was my grandmother's word for them. Nobody lands on Cindermoor while the lights between are dark. She never said what happens when they're lit, because in her day they always were.
Oda wets her thumb on the ink-stick and draws one line, from Kindleby's quay straight into the black in the middle of the chart.
The lane in. The Keepers' boats came out along it the week of the Snuffing; I lay off the Taper and watched them go by. Where boats come out, there's water to go in by.
It's never been a Tidewright lane. Tidewrights don't go to the Spire. The Spire comes to us, or it did.
Say the word and I'll take you in. Not on the next tide because you're in a hurry. When you've said what you've got to say to whoever you're leaving behind.

lane_in.text: She says it like the name of a rock she has spent her whole life steering round.
Keepers pay twice on my deck: once for the crossing and once for the Spire. You've paid me crossings since the Gull. I'd say this is the other one.
I weighed you once, on the Gull's dock. I'll not weigh you again. Whatever you are, you've paid it six times over.
You told the colliers on the Northing's stage you'd tell the Spire they're waiting. Well. Now you can.
Once we're in that water, I'll not be putting back out for anything you forgot. There's no lane off it till the Spire's lit, or till I find one. So. Is there anybody left you owe a word?

choice.text: Nobody I can't owe it to from there. Take me in.
Not yet. There's somebody I've to see first.

lane_in_wait.text: Then go and see them. The Mercy's not going anywhere without you. That's rather the point.

lane_in_go.text: Oda folds the chart along the new line and puts it back inside her coat, next to the scale.
The morning ebb, then. Get some sleep. I'll not.

Up on the crown the Vigil Light burns, and away on the Low Water a small gold point answers it, and the candles go round Kindleby the way they have for nine hundred years. In the middle of the ring, where the chart has always been black, there's nothing to see at all.

lane_in_sail.text: The morning ebb. Kindleby's candles are still lit along the wall, pale in the grey, and somebody is changing them. Oda doesn't make a speech. She looks at the chart once, folds it, and gives the word.
Up at the quay bell Tobin takes the rope in both hands and strokes it once. Then he holds the rope, and doesn't strike again.
One stroke. That's the Keepers' bell for a boat going out to the Spire. You only ever hear the one. The second's for when they come back.
The Provost stands on the quay steps in her red stole. As the Mercy comes off the stage she lifts her hand, and keeps it up.
The Provost stands on the quay steps in her red stole and watches the Mercy as far as the candles. Then she turns and goes up.
Brother Iver is on the wall among the candles, a taper in his hand. He doesn't wave. He watches the water, the way he always has.
On the west wall, between two of her forty, Wenna Coll lifts her rake at you. Ottie is beside her, looking north, and then, for once, east.

Then the candles are behind you, and the fog closes, and there's nothing ahead to steer by. Oda steers by what's astern: the Vigil Light dead aft, and the Wrack Light and Lowsong's small gold point held at the same distance either side.
A ring's got a middle. You find it by the edges.
The fog thickens as you go. It ought to thin, going away from the islands and their people. It doesn't. It gets heavier, and slower, and the Mercy's wake lies on it like a crease in cloth.
Thicker in than out. Like water running downhill to a drain. ...I don't like that. I don't know why I don't like it.

Halfway, you look back. All six of them are there at once, all round the Mercy, small and far: the Gull, the Ridge Light, the Heron, the Wrack, the Vigil Light, Lowsong. Like sitting in the middle of a table laid for somebody.
The crew have gone quiet. Even the deckhand who sings at the ropes has stopped singing.

And then Cindermoor comes up out of the fog all at once, the way an island does when you've been staring too hard: high and bare, black cinder and brown heather going up in long steps to a crown. On the crown, the Hearthspire. Tall, slender, pale stone, the only pale thing on the island. Dark at the top.
Thirty-eight years I've steered round that. It's smaller than I thought. Or I'm bigger.

cindermoor.text: I'll be here. There's no lane off this water till the Spire's lit, and I'll not go looking for one with you up there.
Don't make me come looking for you. I'd only forget what for.
Still here. The Mercy's been creaking all night like she's trying to get my attention.

choice.text: The eighth slip has a boat in it.

cindermoor_merrit.text: He did. Nobody's called me novice. Not even my mother, and she had cause.
Leave him be on that bollard. A man who stays where the boats went from is waiting for one to come back. You don't help a man off that.

cindermoor_slips.text: Eight slips and seven boats. I counted them past the Taper, the week it went dark. I never thought to count what didn't come.
Somebody stayed. Or somebody meant to go and didn't get as far as the water. Either way they're up there, and they've had three months of this fog.

cindermoor_no_lane.text: Off this water? There's no lane. I told you on Kindleby, and I'll tell you here, where you can see why.
She nods out past the Mercy's stern. The fog stands there like a wall somebody has built while you weren't looking. You can't see the six lights at all.

cindermoor_after.text: Still here. The Mercy's ready when you are, and so am I, which is rarer.
cindermoor_after.note: Day 97, the epilogue: Oda at the Boat Stair after the count down. What the night looked like from the Mercy, once; then the lane out.

cindermoor_after.text: I saw it go. Gold, straight up out of the fog, like somebody'd opened a door in the sky and left it open.
Thirty-eight years I've steered round that. Now I'll be steering by it. ...You look like somebody who's put something down. I'll not ask what. It wouldn't stick.
Something went past the Mercy in the night. Out, not in. Like a lot of people walking on a floor that isn't there, and singing, going away.
The crew stood up for it. Nobody told them to. ...The fog's no thinner. But I can see the six lights from here, all six, and I couldn't yesterday.
Still dark up there. I sat up all night deciding whether that was good, and then I remembered I'm a ferry-master, and it isn't mine to decide.
You've still got it, then. I can see it from here, in your hand. Good. I've a use for it.
I said there was no lane off this water till the Spire's lit, or till I found one. Well. Get aboard when you're ready, and we'll see which.

lane_out.text: Oda gives the word, and the Mercy comes off the Boat Stair's quay stern first, the way she came in, and turns.

She doesn't look at the chart. She doesn't need to. Astern, on the crown, the Hearthspire burns, and its light lies down the water ahead of the Mercy like a road somebody has swept. The fog goes back off it the way snow goes off a warm roof.
No lane off this water till the Spire's lit. Well. It's lit.

One by one the six lights come up out of the grey ahead. You try to count them and lose your place at two. Oda counts them for you, under her breath, without being asked: the Gull, the Ridge, the Heron, the Wrack, the Vigil Light, Lowsong.

There's nothing astern to steer by: the Spire's a dark spike against a dark sky. Oda stands at the wheel with her chart folded and looks ahead instead, and ahead, for the first time on this water, are the six lights. All of them, all round the ring, like a table laid.
There. ...They're brighter than they were. Like somebody's sitting up with them.
Your hand on the rail is cold. The black coal in it is only a coal. The fog lies on the water either side, thick as ever, and it lets the Mercy by as if she were nobody it needed anything from.
That's my lane, then. I said I'd find one. I didn't say I'd be the one to find it.
Past the quay's end the fog stands up off the water like a wall. Oda looks at it, and then at your hand.
Go up in the bow. Hold it up.

You go up in the bow and hold the ember up, and the fog parts round it the way it has always parted round you, only wider now, the width of a ferry, and the Mercy goes out down the gap with her lantern swinging.
So that's how you do it. Thirty-eight years. I could have just asked.
By evening the candles of Kindleby's wall are a line of sparks low on the water ahead, and Oda folds the chart along the lane in, and puts it away, and doesn't need it.

lane_out_again.text: The lane out again, down the Spire's light. Oda doesn't make a speech.
The lane out again, between the six lights. Oda doesn't make a speech.
The lane out again, the ember up in the bow. Oda doesn't make a speech.

lane_back_in.text: Back in? ...Aye. I'll not say I like that water. I'll say I know the way now.
The Spire's light comes up out of the fog to meet the Mercy halfway, and she runs in down it to the Boat Stair.
The Mercy runs in down the lane she found coming out, and the Boat Stair comes up out of the fog where it always was.
